## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.

4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?

8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. 🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. topics.title: [eval] Evaluate Hero at multiple context lengths
topics.head: eea42ac9a3a197345bf6f762709fb6aed7c0e0aa
topics.body:
Hero evals score 4K and the current training length, adding fixed 65K and 262K evals only once training reaches those lengths. Each distinct length has its own metrics, such as `eval_dropless/seq_len_4096/paloma/macro_loss`; `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` continues to report the training-length eval.

All eval lengths keep the training context-parallel width. The dropless mesh and PartitionSpec renaming reuse #10709's implementation: each device retains its training context group and uses its training (data, expert) group for eval data. Eval therefore reuses the device groups whose replacement caused NCCL memory growth in #10709. Batch sizes stay within the configured global padded-token budget per evaluation batch, rounded down to whole batch shards.

Continuous-text validation retains incomplete final sequences with right padding and excludes padding from attention and loss, including the real-to-pad prediction. Short Paloma corpora remain in the long-context aggregate. Validation sequence statistics include the final partial sequence; stored token counts exclude padding. Overall loss and bits-per-byte macros exclude tags with no scored tokens.

CPU tests check device groups, per-device parameter shards and the multi-length eval-to-training handoff. No GPU rehearsal of this revision has run.

Part of #8435.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f.

The change scores the hero at 4K, 65K, 262K and the training length at every scheduled eval. It also stops validation from dropping each continuous-text corpus's final partial sequence. The Levanter padding and macro-average changes are sound and well tested. The one design problem is in the hero: the dropless eval for the long lengths runs on a mesh whose device groups training never uses. Open PR #10709 measured that pattern exhausting GB200 memory.

**Before.** `_run_grug_local` built at most two evaluators at a single length: `cb_tagged_evaluate` on the training mesh and a dropless evaluator on `compact_grug_mesh(expert_axis_size=1, context_axis_size=<training CP>)`. `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` could pin that length, but no launcher set it. Validation used `TokenSeqDataset`, which drops the incomplete tail, so a Paloma subset shorter than one sequence (PTB, WikiText-103 at 262K) yielded no examples. The macro then averaged a zero-weight tag into the result.

**Design.** `build_eval_hooks` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:701`) builds one hook per length and backend. Every hook holds the training-length token budget, `eval_batch_size * train_seq_len`. `_dropless_eval_mesh` reshapes each rack's `(data, context, expert)` devices into a wider `context` axis when one sequence per batch shard would exceed that budget. At the 16K hero this yields CP1/CP1/CP4/CP16 for 4K/16K/65K/262K. Metrics go to `<prefix>/seq_len_<n>/…`, and the training-length hook also writes the old unqualified keys. In Levanter, `PaddedTokenSeqDataset` right-pads the tail and adds `valid_tokens`. `CausalLmDataset` turns those into segment ID `-1` and zero loss weight, including the real-to-pad prediction. FA4's packed-segment bounds already treat `-1` as invalid. `TaggedEvaluator` excludes tags with no scored tokens from both macros.

**Evidence and limits.** I ran the new tests locally on CPU and all 11 passed: `test_evaluation.py`, the padded-validation cases in `test_text.py`, and the macro test in `test_eval.py`. The PR body says GPU memory and wall time are unmeasured, and the README asks for a rehearsal before the relaunch. Nothing exercises the CP4/CP16 eval meshes on GPUs, or the `_fa4_cute.py` unit-batch normalization outside its CPU path.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:634` `_dropless_eval_mesh` gives the 65K and 262K evals device groups that 16K CP1 training never uses. The 65K eval has CP4 groups of four adjacent devices and data groups of 16. The 262K eval has CP16 and data 4. Open #10709 (mcwitt) measured this mechanism on the same model. XLA creates an NCCL communicator for each new group, keeps it outside the allocator pool for the rest of the process, and at 65K CP4×EP16 that added about 7.4 GiB per GPU against 5.8 GiB of headroom, so the next train step failed to allocate. Here the two long-length evals each add a new layout at every scheduled eval, so the first eval of the relaunched hero can OOM its next train step. #10709 also rewrites the same dropless-mesh code (`expert_collapsed_eval_mesh` plus a spec-renaming `_reshard_tree_to_mesh`), so the two PRs conflict. Land #10709 first, then rebase this PR onto its fold for each length whose context width equals training's. Keep 65K and 262K out of `HERO_FIXED_EVAL_SEQ_LENS` (`hero_recipe.py:35`) until a one-rack rehearsal records non-pool memory across those evals and the next train step. If a raised-CP length does not fit, score it from checkpoints in a separate eval job.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py:562` `remainder` defaults to `"drop"`, and `count_corpus_sizes` (`datasets.py:1414`) still builds validation sets without it. So `data/stats/validation/<name>/total_seqs` now counts one sequence fewer than the evaluator scores for every corpus with a partial tail, and zero for the short Paloma subsets this PR keeps. Make `remainder` a required keyword, as AGENTS.md asks for critical parameters, and pass `remainder="pad"` for the validation loop in `count_corpus_sizes`.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f -->

🤖 Removed stale expert-collapsed wording from the shared eval hook. The two review findings change behavior and remain open. Pre-commit, 11 focused CPU cases, and lint review passed. Commit 70df5e5f93.

<!-- marin-deslop:cde42d80d99bc348177d5ebfeb3d508cd757098f -->

🤖 Addressed finding 2 in 8c33ae5f38: `remainder` is now required, all callers specify the policy, and validation corpus statistics use padding. The full text suite passes (40 cases), including short, exact-length and partial-tail corpus statistics; lint and Pyrefly pass.

Finding 1 remains a production blocker. #10709 provides measured evidence that new eval device groups can retain enough NCCL memory to OOM the next training step. I have documented that blocker in the PR body and README. The requested four lengths remain configured, and no run has been relaunched. This needs group reuse coordinated with #10709 and a GPU rehearsal before production use; the CPU round-trip tests do not establish that memory acceptance.

🤖 Addressed the remaining device-group finding in 4cbdb820f2. Dropless eval now uses #10709's `expert_collapsed_eval_mesh` and PartitionSpec renaming, with one fixed layout for all lengths. Its group/shard regression test is included, and the real multi-length round-trip test now runs at a fixed training CP2 layout. Hero no longer requests eval lengths above the training length: the current configuration evaluates 4K and 16K; 65K and 262K are added only after training reaches them.

The affected CPU suite passed 3,578 tests; its only failure is the same Linux-only bubblewrap case previously reproduced on base. Lint/Pyrefly passed. Advisory review's one docstring finding was corrected in eea42ac9a3. No GPU job or relaunch was run; the PR body states that limit.

I am wondering how much 'keeping the final partial chunk' is going to change the data used for the 4k and 16k evals. I think it would be good to test these on 1 rack for the existing checkpoints- if there is a noticeable gap in macro loss we'd want to keep the current behavior for 4k and 16k context length, so that the eval uses the same data we used during the forecast.

topics.title: [eval] Preserve partial SkyRL rollout results
topics.head: 999bf7d5676719215984dc091b5116a781dad5e5
topics.body:
Append completed SkyRL eval rollouts locally and periodically upload a consistent scored prefix to two fixed backup keys per attempt. Each snapshot records its attempt and completed/expected rollout counts. A supervised background process has a 30-second upload deadline; storage failures are logged while evaluation continues.

A retry uses new backup keys and preserves earlier attempt prefixes. Step-wise rows carry `is_last_step` in both partial and full dumps so readers can select the rows used for metrics. Snapshots are best effort and can miss rollouts completed since the last successful backup; the existing per-dataset and aggregate files remain full-evaluation outputs.

The partial-prefix and retry regressions pass locally, and the `marinskyrl` wheel build contains the new recorder.

Fixes #10837

comments.body: Working on this in loom: https://loom.oa.dev/s/ebhejzv8

🤖 Holistic review of 644e29c07350ced087bea71cb4c4d91cdfe29e23.

This change keeps a scored prefix of a SkyRL evaluation when the job dies before the final dump. The design matches the maintainer's request on #10837: best-effort writes with a bounded timeout, never failing the eval. Two gaps remain. A retried attempt erases the earlier attempt's snapshots, and step-wise snapshots contain rows that the final dump drops.

**Before.** `_collect_evaluation_rollouts` held every `TrajectoryBatch` in memory. `dump_per_dataset_eval_results` wrote `{dataset}.jsonl` and `aggregated_results.jsonl` only after the last rollout returned. A timeout at 94% (the Mini840 run in #10837) left nothing under `dumped_evals/`.

**After.** When `trainer.dump_eval_results` is set, each completed rollout is serialized with the new shared `evaluation_result_entries`, the row schema the final dump now also uses. `PartialEvaluationRecorder` appends those rows plus a `progress` record to a local JSONL file. Every 25 rollouts or 300 seconds, a supervisor thread starts a spawned process. That process copies the flushed byte prefix behind a `partial_evaluation` header (attempt ID, completed/expected rollouts, `snapshot_at`) and uploads it to `partial-0.jsonl` or `partial-1.jsonl`. The process is killed after 30 seconds. The slot flips only after a successful upload, so a timed-out write never replaces the last good object. `close()` runs in the collector's `finally` and makes one final bounded backup, so a failed `TaskGroup` still leaves its prefix. Every recorder error is logged and evaluation continues.

**Evidence.** `infra/tests/test_partial_evaluation.py` runs in the `skyrl-wheel` CI leg and passed locally. It covers out-of-order appends, repetition IDs, counts, and the local publish path through the spawned process. It does not cover `io.upload_file` (cloud targets), the `evaluate.py` wiring, or step-wise batches. The blocked-upload deadline probe and wheel-content check are claims in the PR body; nothing in the repository reproduces them.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix:** `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py:134` Both slots use fixed keys under the session directory, which is the same path for every Iris retry. `iris_backend.py` sets no `max_retries_preemption`, so preempted SkyRL jobs retry by default. The retry's first rollout immediately triggers a backup into slot 0, and its next successful backup (at 25 rollouts or 5 minutes) overwrites slot 1. A run preempted at 94% therefore loses its 94% prefix within minutes of restarting, and loses it permanently if the retry also dies. The docs (`docs/dev-guide/skyrl.md:38`) tell readers to pick a snapshot "for an attempt", but at most one older-attempt object survives, and only briefly. Include the attempt ID in the target names (`partial-<attempt_id>-{0,1}.jsonl`, created in `PartialEvaluationRecorder` or passed in from `evaluate.py`). This still costs two objects per attempt and matches the attempt-specific prefix proposed in #10837. Then update the docs paragraph.
- **2. Should fix:** `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py:180` On step-wise evaluation (`trainer.step_wise_training`, used by `experiments/post_training/task_sessions/validation.py`), every step row is appended with an `is_last_step` flag. `evaluate_step_wise` filters to last-step rows before dumping and scoring. A reader who averages `score` over a partial snapshot, which the docs imply, averages intermediate-step rewards that the final per-dataset JSONL never contains, and `trajectory_rows` counts them too. Append only the `is_last_step` rows so snapshots match the final dump's row set. This also removes the extra `is_last_step` key from the schema.
- **3. Related PR:** #10737 adds `task_id` to the inline entry dict that this PR moves into `evaluation_result_entries` (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/trainer_utils.py:331`). Whichever lands second must add `task_id` to the shared helper so partial and final rows keep one schema. Do not restore the inline dict.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:644e29c07350ced087bea71cb4c4d91cdfe29e23 -->

🤖 Removed an assertion that only compared expected rollouts with the value passed into the recorder. Changed-files lint and the narrow SkyRL test pass. The review's two behavior findings remain open.

<!-- marin-deslop:644e29c07350ced087bea71cb4c4d91cdfe29e23 -->

🤖 Addressed the retry overwrite in `58b5874a94`: each attempt now has its own pair of backup keys, and the retry regression verifies the earlier snapshot remains intact.

For step-wise eval, `evaluate_step_wise` filters final-step rows for metrics but passes the unfiltered `rollouts` to the full dump. Both dumps now retain all step rows with `is_last_step` in the shared row format; the docs say to select final-step rows when deriving scores. A persisted-output regression covers the marker.

PR #10737 is still open. Its `task_id` field will need to move into the shared serializer if that PR lands first.

topics.title: [hero] Switch the hero run from 16K to 65K context
topics.body:
This issue tracks switching the hero run ([#8435](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8435)) from 16K to 65K (65,536-token) context. Run status lives in [#8506](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8506); the 16K switch was [#9615](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9615) and [#10101](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10101).

**Plan.** Hand off at **permanent step-372000** of 390,251, which the live run writes near **Mon 11-02 03:00 UTC (Sun 11-01 19:00 PST)**, and launch 65K that night; the fallback is Mon 11-02 ~09:00 PST from the same checkpoint. Run 65K on the 16K mesh, CP1 × EP64, with capacity factor 1.5 and qk_mult 1.66. The critical path is the deploy PR ([#10820](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10820), B1) and its one-rack test (C1).

**Status (11-02 04:03 UTC): GO.** `hero-ctx65k-step372k` launched at 03:25 UTC from `6e6924fedd`, restored step-372000 and passed every F2 gate at step 372,102 on its first attempt: median 16.05 s/step, drop fraction ~3.5e-4, peak HBM 127.8 GiB, loss 0.020 below the parent's over the control window. Projected finish ~Thu 11-05 15:00 UTC. Details: [comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10821#issuecomment-6568749068), [W&B cutover report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/hero-ctx65k-step372k:-65K-context-cutover-at-step-372,000--VmlldzoxODIzOTYyMw==).

## Timing

On 11-01 we chose step-372000, 0.84T tokens (4.7%) at 65K, over step-366000 (1.12T, finishing Sat 11-07) and a manual checkpoint at Monday's relaunch (0.68T), so the 262K extension can finish this week. #8435 planned the last ~5%; Marin's 67B-A2B trained its last 1T of 10T tokens at 65K. Step, token and LR fractions coincide, since every step has 46,137,344 tokens and LR decays linearly.

| Handoff | Step | Tokens left at 65K | Finish at 65K (UTC) | Finish at 16K (UTC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon 11-02 03:00 UTC (tonight) | 372,000 (95.3%) | 0.84T | Thu 11-05 ~17:30 | Thu 11-05 ~03:00 |
| Mon 11-02 17:00 UTC (fallback) | 372,000, discarding ~3,500 16K steps | 0.84T | Fri 11-06 ~07:30 | |

Estimates use the live run's 14.19 s/step since its 10-30 launch, including checkpoint writes, ~16.8 s/step at 65K with the same overhead, and ~1.25 h for the switch.

## Configuration

One GB200 rack, restored from step-300000, 500 steps per arm, same code, run back to back:

| Arm | s/step | Drop fraction | Peak HBM (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [CP4 × EP16, capacity factor 1.15](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp4-01) | 14.699 | 2.41e-3 | 127.6 |
| [CP1 × EP64, capacity factor 1.5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp1cf15-01) | 15.397 | 9.80e-4 | 128.4 |

- **CP1 × EP64 (decided 10-31).** It is 4.7% slower per step than CP4, about 3 h over the rest of the run. It drops 2.5× fewer assignments, needs no launcher change, and its dropless eval passes on main with 12.3 GiB free per GPU. CP4's eval crashes the next train step on main until [#10709](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10709) merges. CP4 work ([#10618](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10618), #10709) continues for the 262K extension.
- **Capacity factor 1.5,** up from the hero's 1.15. At 1.0, CP1 at 65K drops 1.9% of assignments.
- **qk_mult 1.66,** the 262K formula 1.3 × (0.1·ln(65536/4096) + 1).
- **Throughput (estimate):** ~16.3 s/step on the hero, −15% tok/s against 16K.
- **Skipped tokens:** ~50B at the switch, as each data source skips the rest of its shuffle window; 52.2B at the 16K switch.

## Risks

1. The production launcher has never run 65K; it always runs the hero on 11 racks, so every 65K measurement, including C1, used the one-rack `launch_diagnostics`, which shares its trainer config but not the context history.
2. Capacity factor 1.5 has never run at 11 racks; drops and step time are first measured at the deploy.
3. Peak HBM is 128.4 GiB, against 123.4 GiB at 16K and a 143.75 GiB allocator limit.
4. Eight hero racks run an old IMEX revision that keeps GPU memory imported from a departed peer, which made the 10-29 retries OOM. They are swept while the hero is stopped (G3).
5. Nothing evaluates the hero past 32K ([#7638](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638)), so the 65K phase is judged on loss alone.

## Checklist

N is the handoff step.

### A. Decisions

- [x] **A1** Handoff at permanent step-372000, launched tonight once the parent logs step 372,049, near Mon 11-02 03:15 UTC (decided 11-01). Monday ~09:00 PST from the same checkpoint is the fallback.
- [x] **A2** CP1 × EP64, capacity factor 1.5, qk_mult 1.66 (decided 10-31).
- [x] **A3** Gates agreed 11-01; see F2.

### B. Code

topics.title: [eval] A job timeout mid-eval discards every rollout result
topics.body:
An eval that is killed before its last rollout writes no results at all. `evaluate()` in `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py` collects every rollout for the whole eval set in `_collect_evaluation_rollouts` and calls `_dump_eval_results` once, at `evaluate.py:235`, after all rows return. `dump_per_dataset_eval_results` (`skyrl_train/utils/trainer_utils.py:331`) then rewrites each `{dataset}.jsonl` in `"w"` mode. Eval-only launches keep no resumable checkpoint (`resume_path: null`), so a timeout, preemption, or crash loses every rollout, including the ones that already finished.

Observed on `mini840-e2e-qwen35-35b-a3b-base@2026.10.31.23`: 1,522/1,626 rollouts (94%) after 71,580s against an 86,400s `config.iris.timeout`. `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/checkpoints/mini840-e2e-qwen35-35b-a3b-base/2026.10.31.23/exports/` was still empty, so a timeout with about 100 rollouts left would have discarded the other 1,500 and left no numbers for the model.

Trajectory retention does not cover the gap. That run used `sample_fraction: 0.0` with `always_retain_failures/loops/non_terminating: true`, so its 401 uploaded `installed-agents/` trials are failure-shaped and non-random against 1,522 completed rollouts.

Reproduce:
1. Launch an eval-only SkyRL run whose wall clock exceeds the job timeout. The Mini840 launcher sets `job_timeout_seconds` in `experiments/evaluation/mini_policy_runtime/launch.py`; set it below the expected run length.
2. Wait until the eval progress line passes 90%.
3. Cancel the job and list the export path. No `dumped_evals/` directory exists.

Expected: completed rollouts survive the kill. Dump each finished batch, or each finished row, with an explicit partial marker and rollout count, so an interrupted eval leaves a scored prefix that can be audited.

The change belongs in `vendor/skyrl` (`evaluate.py`), which ships in the eval runtime wheel, so the fix needs a wheel rebuild rather than only a launcher change.

comments.body: @weaverbot can you propose a fix? Seems like we could do something pretty limited in scope that would address this, like having Finelog detect when vendor/skyrl is running an eval and preserve it as we do with our other vendored eval framework traces.
~~On it~~ — this session was relaunched; the live status card is below.

🤖
## Research

[`_collect_evaluation_rollouts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/aea328e4281c7094f5452d9c5d45294aaad95200/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py#L108-L175) gathers all requests before [`evaluate()` writes results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/aea328e4281c7094f5452d9c5d45294aaad95200/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py#L277-L303). The [shared dumper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/aea328e4281c7094f5452d9c5d45294aaad95200/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/trainer_utils.py#L331-L405) overwrites dataset JSONL and aggregate metrics after collection, so a kill before that point leaves no scored output. Repeatedly calling it during collection would rewrite growing cloud objects; [`io.write_bytes_atomic`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/aea328e4281c7094f5452d9c5d45294aaad95200/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/io/io.py#L98-L110) already supports single-object publication.

## Proposed Fix

1. Start each evaluation with a `partial` status record containing an attempt ID and expected request count. Keep partial data under an attempt-specific prefix so a retry cannot mix with an earlier run.
2. After each request finishes, serialize its scored trajectory rows using the same row schema as the final dump. Write one immutable object keyed by input row and repetition through a bounded background writer; await publication before counting it as persisted. A write failure must fail the evaluation.
3. Expose persisted request and trajectory counts from committed objects. Refresh the progress record after writes, but have the audit reader reconcile counts from objects if a kill lands between the data and progress writes. Keep aggregate scores and the existing per-dataset JSONL files as complete-evaluation outputs; publish `complete` only after those files are written.
4. Add a local filesystem regression that cancels after a scored prefix and checks its scores, IDs, counts, and `partial` state. Cover out-of-order completions, repetitions, and step-wise batches; verify the existing final files on successful completion. Run the SkyRL CPU tests and wheel packaging check before release.

This spans the shared collector, cloud publication, and the output contract, so it needs a reviewed change rather than a launcher-only edit. [PR #10737](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10737) changes nearby evaluation metrics and should be accounted for when implementing; [PR #10817](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10817) supplies the Mini840 launcher.

🤖 Proposed narrow fix: persist results at the SkyRL rollout completion point in `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/evaluate.py`.

Finelog can retain progress that SkyRL emits, but detecting an eval from its logs cannot recover the scored `TrajectoryBatch` rows currently held only in memory. The retained `installed-agents/` trials are also a selected subset. I would keep Finelog for visibility and make the eval export the source of record:

1. In `_collect_evaluation_rollouts.collect`, after `pool.run` returns and the row is validated, serialize that row using the existing `dump_per_dataset_eval_results` schema (UID, dataset, repetition, score, response, verification, error fields). Write it to a unique immutable object under `dumped_evals/<session>/partial_rows/<validation-source>/<row-index>-<repetition>.json`, and await the write before advancing the progress bar. Use the existing cloud/local `io.write_bytes_atomic` helper; do not append to or repeatedly rewrite an S3 JSONL object. A failed upload should fail the eval rather than count an unpreserved row as complete.
2. Create a `partial` manifest before launching rollouts with the expected rollout count. Treat the committed row objects as the authoritative completed count, so a kill between a row upload and a manifest update cannot overstate or lose results. After all rows finish, keep the current per-dataset JSONL and aggregate output, then publish a `complete` marker with the final count. An interrupted run has the partial marker, its exact committed-row count, and no full-eval marker.
3. Report any score recovered from a partial run as `completed/expected` (and scored/attempted), never as the full benchmark result. For `eval_n_samples_per_prompt > 1`, compute `pass@n` only from prompts with all repetitions present.

A regression test can hold the final rollout open, cancel `evaluate()` after several earlier rollouts have finished, and assert those rows are readable with partial status and the correct count. A successful run should still produce the existing final files and a complete marker. The changed vendored SkyRL code must be rebuilt into the eval runtime wheel before a launch can use it.

@weaverbot S3 is too flaky to reliably sustain a unique immutable object for every serialized write and it's overkill anyway. We definitely shouldn't freeze or fail a job in flight over this, SkyRL evals are not supposed to be canonical. Let's have best effort writes with a bounded timeout, async so they don't block progress, and appending a pre-allocated file with periodic backups to another pre-allocated file so we don't have to make as many s3 calls. Please put together a PR for it, thanks.

On it — https://loom.oa.dev/s/ebhejzv8

- 🟠 `Nov  2 11:32Z` **attention** — Fix proposed for #10837; design review requested: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10837#issuecomment-6576082544
- 🟢 `Nov  2 11:46Z` Implementing bounded asynchronous partial eval backups for issue #10837
- 🟠 `Nov  2 11:57Z` **attention** — PR #10840 open for review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10840
- 🟠 `Nov  2 12:13Z` **attention** — PR #10840 green; awaiting review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10840

🤖 Revised plan after the S3 feedback: append each completed, scored rollout to a local JSONL file. A background worker will periodically copy a consistent prefix and upload it to alternating fixed backup keys under `dumped_evals`, with a hard upload deadline. Each backup will state `partial`, its completed/expected rollout counts, and its attempt ID; readers can use the newest valid backup. Backup failures will be logged and will not stop evaluation. The existing full-eval dump remains the completion output. I’ll add a cancellation regression and verify the vendored wheel includes the change.

🤖 Opened [PR #10840](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10840) to retain scored SkyRL eval prefixes. Completed rollouts append to a local JSONL file; a background process periodically uploads consistent snapshots to two fixed backup keys and stops an upload after 30 seconds. Each snapshot records `partial`, its attempt ID, and completed/expected rollout counts. Backup failures leave the eval running; a kill can still lose results since the last successful backup.

The Python 3.12 partial-prefix regression, a blocked-upload deadline probe, and the rebuilt `marinskyrl` wheel check passed. Advisory review found no issues. CI and PR review are in progress.

🤖 [PR #10840](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10840) is open with green CI, including `skyrl-wheel`. Completed eval rollouts append locally; a background process periodically uploads a scored prefix to two fixed backup keys per attempt, with a 30-second deadline. A retry keeps the prior attempt’s snapshots. Each snapshot identifies its attempt and completed/expected rollout counts. Step-wise rows carry `is_last_step` so partial scores can use the same final-step selection as eval metrics.

Backups are best effort: a kill may lose rollouts since the last successful upload, and storage errors do not stop the eval. Local partial-prefix and retry tests passed; the step-wise persisted-output test passed in CI. The PR awaits human review.

topics.title: [datakit] Mark documents that hold most of one eval item
topics.head: 0f937b6001aec6b35e420b64f62f525fb553e345
topics.body:
Decon marking gains an item rule, OR-ed with the paragraph rule: a record is also marked when it holds at least a share T of one eval item's indexed 13-grams, wherever they sit in the record. The paragraph rule scores each paragraph by the share of its own n-grams that hit the filter, so an eval item inside a long paragraph (a JSON line, a code file, a quiz page) scores low and survives. The item rule scores the item instead, so surrounding text cannot dilute it.

`ItemMatchConfig` takes `(eval_id_prefix, T)` pairs; items outside every prefix are left to the paragraph rule. The reference pipeline and testbed enable it for the core and Uncheatable evals: T=0.5 for MMLU, MMLU-Pro and Uncheatable, 0.4 for HumanEval and 0.3 for GSM8K, whose copies often omit the tests or the worked answer. Drop-set n-grams do not count toward T but stay in the item's n-gram count, so boilerplate and templates cannot carry an item over the bar. Matched items are written to a new `matched_eval_ids` column, and `DECON_ATTRIBUTES_VERSION` moves to 6.

The corpus now indexes each lm-eval item as two records: the harness prompt with its target, and the raw string fields one per line, without grader fields (`test`, `test_list`). v5 joined both into one record, so a training copy of either rendering held only part of it. `EVAL_CORPUS_VERSION` moves to aa-index-v4.1.1-v6.

Only paragraphs that contain a backslash are JSON-unescaped, in bounded pieces, so multi-GB records do not need several full unescaped copies.

The v6 corpus is not yet staged in the regional prefixes that hold v5; the Datakit canaries need it there before merge.

Part of #6852

🤖 Holistic review of 7a8e019e50bb6f8a55830b72b5e676c5f49b5d2a.

This PR adds an item rule to Datakit decon marking. A record is now also marked when it contains at least a share T of one eval item's indexed 13-grams. The PR also re-cuts the lm-eval corpus so that each doc gives two records, the harness prompt and the raw fields. The core logic is sound and the new tests cover the rule's behavior. The new `matched_eval_ids` column is written but never read: the report and the viewer still attribute marks only through `matched_hashes`, so documents marked only by the item rule appear in them with no eval attached.

**Before.** `_document_overlap_and_matches` scored each paragraph by the share of its own n-grams that hit the bloom. An eval item inside a long JSON line or code file was diluted by the text around it and was not marked. The `eval_hash_index.parquet` sidecar was read only by the report and the viewer, to map `matched_hashes` back to eval ids.

**Design.** `_scan_document` now also collects every bloom hit, including drop-set hits. `_matched_items` adds hits from paragraphs that contain a backslash, after undoing JSON escapes in pieces of at most 16M characters. It then subtracts the drop set and calls `_ItemIndex.matched_eval_ids`. That index is the sidecar loaded once per process into sorted numpy arrays, so it is exact and bloom false positives never count. Each item's size is its row count, and drop-set n-grams stay in that size, so boilerplate alone cannot carry an item over T. A longest-prefix lookup assigns each item its threshold; an item that no prefix covers gets infinity. `ItemMatchConfig` enters the step hash, and `DECON_ATTRIBUTES_VERSION` and `EVAL_CORPUS_VERSION` both move. The record ids `<task>-<split>-<i>` and `<task>-<split>-<i>-fields` stay distinct, so the "index rows are distinct (hash, eval_id) pairs" assumption behind `sizes` holds.

**Evidence and limits.** The recall and precision counts on a 0.5% sample of the training store, and the 11.1 GB peak on a 1.5G-character record, are claims in the PR body; nothing checked into the repo reproduces them. Locally, `tests/datakit` passes at this head (527 passed, 5 xfailed). The body says the v6 corpus is not yet staged in the regional prefixes, so the Datakit canaries cannot pass until it is. This PR is stacked on #10541 and merges after it.

**Findings**

- **1. Should fix:** `experiments/datakit/reports/decontam.py:72` The decontam report and the viewer (`experiments/datakit/decontam/viewer/export_run.py:164`, `:191`, `:311`) still read only `matched_hashes` to attribute a flagged document to evals. An item-rule-only mark has empty `matched_hashes`, so it shows up in the sampled flagged rows with no families, no matched eval text and no `eval_hits` entry. `n_evals_hit` undercounts the evals that the item rule catches, and those are the HumanEval and MMLU copies this PR exists to catch. Read `matched_eval_ids` from the flagged sidecar in both places and count each id toward `hits`, the families, and `matched_evals`, for example with a fixed weight or the item's matched-hash count.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py:2230` `decon_step` accepts `item_match` with `ngram_length=None` and then drops it, because `NGramConfig` is built only when `ngram_length is not None`. The value still enters `hash_attrs`, so an exact-paragraph step silently runs without the item rule under a hash that names it. Raise `ValueError` when `item_match` is set without `ngram_length`, as the docstring's "Needs an n-gram config" implies. The new docstring entry also landed inside the `paragraph_delimiter` entry, so "When reusing a `prebuilt_bloom`, MUST match the delimiter…" now reads as part of `item_match`. Move the `item_match` entry below that sentence.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:7a8e019e50bb6f8a55830b72b5e676c5f49b5d2a -->

🤖 Removed stale v5 wording, a transient issue reference, and an inaccurate comment on piece size; moved the delimiter warning under its parameter. Changed-files lint passed; Datakit: 527 passed, 5 xfailed. Behavioral findings remain with the author.

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 65K context at permanent step 372000
topics.head: eb73ef71212079d53179a3763295dfa912374c35
topics.body:
The hero trains at 65,536-token context from permanent step-372000 of `hero-gradclip-step356k`, on the same CP1 × EP64 mesh as at 16K, with qk_mult 1.66 and receiver capacity factor 1.5 (up from 1.15). Each rack keeps 4,194,304 tokens per update, so the 11-rack batch is 704 sequences. The 16K phase is appended to the hero's context history with the parent's cumulative FLOPs at step 372000, and the launch record names the child run, handoff checkpoint and W&B fork point. That leaves 18,251 steps (4.7%, 0.84T tokens) at 65K.

`HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 projected to W&B `_step` 371999: the parent adds the same FLOPs every 16K step, and projecting from `_step` 359999 matches the logged total at 369975 to 8e-13. The logged value is checked against it before launch.

On one GB200 rack at 65K, CP1 with capacity factor 1.5 ran at 15.397 s/step with drop fraction 9.80e-4 and peak HBM 128.4 GiB, against 14.699 s, 2.41e-3 and 127.6 GiB for CP4 × EP16, over 500 steps each; its dropless eval completes. CP1 at capacity factor 1.0 drops 1.9% of assignments. qk_mult 1.66 is 1.3 × (0.1 ln(65536/4096) + 1). The one-rack test of this branch ([`tok350-deploy65k-c1-01`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-deploy65k-c1-01)), restored from step-360000, ran 60 steps at 15.571 s/step median with drop fraction 8.29e-4 and peak HBM 127.9 GiB; three dropless evals completed (Paloma macro loss 1.995–1.998) with no OOM or retry. Its step is 1.1% slower than the earlier arm's; this branch includes the gradient clipping of #10783, which that arm predated. A 100-step rehearsal from step-366000 ran at 15.518 s/step median with peak HBM 127.9 GiB through two checkpoint saves.

Part of #8435; tracked in #10821.

topics.title: Hero Run Checkpoint Prompt Completions
topics.body: Issue to track prompt completions across checkpoints. Main purpose is just a sanity check on learning. But also to have some fun seeing what the model is learning.

comments.body:
🤖 Prompt completions across three permanent checkpoints — **step-6000, step-24000, step-42000** — sampled at temperature 0.2. Each prompt is sampled independently (own batch row, own position) in one forward per step; `⟨EOS⟩` = ended naturally, `⟨cut at max_new_tokens⟩` = hit the 200-token cap. Two prompt sets: code/open-ended (seed 0) and factual lists (seed 1).

## Code / open-ended prompts (temp 0.2, seed 0)

### `def add_two_numbers(x, y):`
_(temp 0.2)_

**6k** ⟨cut at max_new_tokens⟩
```
def add_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x + y  

def subtract_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x - y  

def multiply_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x * y  

def divide_two_numbers(x, y):  
    if y == 0:  
        raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero.")  
    return x / y  

def main():  
    print("Welcome to the Calculator!")  
    while True:
```

```
    smallest_prime = None

        if num > 1:
            for i in range(2, num):
                if (num % i) == 0:
                    break
            else:
                if smallest_prime is None or num < smallest_prime:
                    smallest_prime = num
```

[grug] Ragged EP train step hangs silently on one rack at d6144 hero scale
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

comments.body:
🤖 The mechanism this issue describes is not what the hung run did, and the root cause is still open. Recording what has been ruled out so the next attempt does not repeat it.

The hero had one train executable, not two alternating ones. `launch_scaling_ladder.py:216` sets `WatchMode.INLINE` at the deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca`, so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built (`train.py:906`), `jit_train_step` computes watch stats on every step, and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. Step 54071 was byte-identical to 54070 at the XLA and NCCL level. The working pooled-wave hero carries the identical watch config and does not hang.

The capacity-limited evaluator was already disabled. `c3f51e5250` (#8859) is an ancestor of `8e48cdb3ca`, and the dropless evaluator uses `sonic_cute`, which has no all-to-all and registers no symmetric window.

Window aliasing is present but was not the trigger. Two `jit_train_step` executables per rank each register a window at `0xbf80000000`; the cause is now known and is a step-counter sharding mismatch (details in #8861). What turns that aliasing into the `ncclGroupEnd` error is a third executable with a smaller footprint, and no such executable was running here.

Ruled out with evidence, all on one rack at the hero's shape, data and checkpoint unless noted. GIN: the device kernel logs `lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152 num_updates_per_replica=6`, and forcing `lsa_size < num_ranks` produces `Device kernel skipped: lsa_size=32 num_ranks=64 requires GIN` followed by a hard `RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed`, so `SupportsGin()` is false in this configuration. That also proves every hero EP domain was a single NVLink domain, since a domain spanning two would have failed loudly rather than stalled. CTA co-residency: the LSA barrier is per-slot, not grid-cooperative — `blockIdx.x` selects a barrier slot and CTA k rendezvouses only with CTA k on its peers — and at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)` the 152-CTA grid uses a fraction of the device, so `0de14631ea` did not regress residency and the comment in that patch claiming the whole grid must be resident is wrong. `core_count` divergence: every rank reports `cta_count=152`. Hardware: the task-index-to-node map is identical across both attempts and the two stuck 16-task slices share no node. Allocator address churn: `Buffer allocations changed address between module jit_train_step executions` fires only for `parameter` and `live-out` entries, never `temp`, so the arena backing the window is stable. Ragged metadata: `CheckRaggedAllToAllBounds` passed 160 of 160 checks on the same HLO operands the device kernel consumes. NCCL 2.31.2: tested, identical failure (see #8861).

One rack does not reproduce it. Attempts covered two 32-GPU EP domains in one rack (161 steps, clean), raised collective overlap (dies of NaN at step 2, which is #8317's corruption and a different regime), NCCL channel contention, forcing the GIN branch, and a full-fidelity control at 48 layers with mixture data restored from the same `step-54000` checkpoint. The remaining differences at eleven racks — cross-rack collectives sharing the GPUs, and a 704-rank communicator — cannot be built inside one NVLink domain.

What survives is a stall in the LSA barrier that cannot report itself. XLA calls `ncclLsaBarrierSession::sync` in the no-timeout form, and NCCL sets `abortFlag` only `if (isInternal)` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1175`), so a user-created devComm has none and no watchdog, abort or CUDA error can fire. The barrier epoch is an absolute counter that persists across launches and is zeroed once at `ncclDevCommCreate`, so any divergence is permanent.

Three instrumentation gaps made both attempts undiagnosable, and should be fixed before the next one. The stall diagnostic is never wired: `train.py:968` calls `progress_watchdog.create(process_index=...)` with no `diagnostic=`, so `diagnostic_timeout` stays unset and the stall capture publishes nothing. If it were wired it would run on the wrong process, because `ProgressWatchdogConfig.create` returns `None` for the entire watchdog when `diagnostic_timeout` is set and `process_index != 0`. And the watchdog's `startup_grace_period` defaulted to one hour, which covered attempt 1's entire hang — that run was killed by hand, not by the watchdog.

For the next eleven-rack attempt: set `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0` alongside `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=3,nccl_symmetric_memory=3,gpu_executable=5`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT,COLL`. `TF_CPP_VMODULE` alone emits nothing, and `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` emits nothing for this failure class. A diagnostic PJRT build on `marin-community/xla` branch `mcwitt/8870-barrier-timeout` bounds both LSA barrier waits with NCCL's timeout overloads and records the stalled rank, barrier slot and phase, so the next occurrence names itself instead of producing fifteen minutes of silence. It also builds the device kernels against the NCCL the runtime loads: `tensorflow.bazelrc` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION=2.29.7` while the runtime installs 2.30.7, and the timeout API exists only in the newer headers.

🤖 Follow-up on one hypothesis worth keeping open: that this is the same class of bug as #8861, namely a sharding JAX infers rather than one the code specifies, going wrong only once `replica_dcn` is a real axis.

Partial test on one rack. A single rack can make that axis non-degenerate by splitting into several expert domains, so: `--expert-axis-size 32` (giving `replica_dcn=2`) with `--num-experts 192` to keep six local experts per GPU and the hero's memory profile, 48 layers, inline watch, with the #8861 step-counter fix applied. Result was 64 arena windows, 64 `jit(train_step)` compilations across 64 ranks, and a per-leaf `Format` diff reporting `identical across the step`. No second state-sharding mismatch appears when the replica axis becomes real, and the #8861 fix holds there.

That does not close the hypothesis. It covers the train state only, at replica width 2, inside one NVLink domain and one process group. It does not cover batch sharding over `_BATCH_AXES = ("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")`, intermediates inside the step, or device ordering across 704 devices in 176 processes. Ordering is the part that matters here: `compact_grug_mesh` builds the mesh by reshaping `jax.devices()` in process order, while a `GSPMDSharding` carries the client's default device order, and the two coincide trivially when `replica_dcn=1`. A disagreement that resolves differently on different racks is the only proposed source of rank-dependent behaviour that survives, which is what a failure hitting one rack of eleven — a different one on each attempt — requires.

The direct test is a dump comparison, and it was not possible before now. `hero_grug_trainer_config` left `sharding_dump_path=None`, so `dump_grug_state_sharding_run_artifact` wrote to the pod-local `logs/` directory and the hung run's dump died with its pod. The ladder now writes it under the run's output path, so the next multi-rack run leaves a dump that can be diffed against a one-rack dump directly. That needs no special build and costs nothing.

Also worth recording for anyone reproducing this: `--expert-axis-size 32` at the hero's 384 experts puts twelve local experts on each GPU instead of six and OOMs at 158 GiB. Halve the expert count to hold the per-GPU profile fixed.

🤖 An eleven-rack reproduction attempt on 2026-09-03 did not reproduce the hang, but it eliminated data- and state-dependence by direct measurement and turned up a version skew that reframes the failure. Root cause is still open.

**The reproduction was faithful, and it did not hang.** Two jobs at 11 racks, 235 steps in total (164 then 71), restored from the same `step-54000` both failed attempts used, at the hero's exact shape. It matched attempt 0's loss to ±0.00007 nats over the whole overlapping range and sat -0.0058 nats against the pooled-wave control, reproducing the -0.006 offset reported above; MFU 22-23% against attempt 0's 23.4%. It carried the same transport (`lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152`) and the same symmetric-window aliasing this issue describes: 1408 arena-window registrations across 704 ranks, exactly two per rank, alongside 1408 `jit_train_step` compilations.

**The hang is not a function of the data or the model state.** Attempt 0 completed step 54071 (`train_loss` 1.23687 at 00:23:35.14Z) and hung on the next one. The replay ran through that step and kept going. Since the loss agrees to seven significant figures, the batch, the routing, the optimizer state and the arithmetic there are identical to the run that died. Combined with attempt 1 hanging at 54001 from the same restored state, the trigger is timing, not state, and the failure cannot be forced by choosing a checkpoint or a step.

**On the statistics, stated carefully.** Hero exposure was 75 step-attempts with two hangs; the reproduction ran 235 clean. A one-sided test gives p ≈ 0.06 — suggestive that something differs between the two setups, but not significant. Job-steps are the right unit here, not rack-steps: the hang is a job-level event, so counting all 11 racks as independent trials overstates the evidence.

**Candidates eliminated since the last update.** Concurrent checkpoint I/O: `grep "Saving checkpoint"` across every task log in both attempts returns zero hits, so neither attempt ever wrote a checkpoint. Online W&B: per-step tracker cost was 3.73-3.84 ms at every detail step and the wandb thread was idle in `selectors.select` at the py-spy dump. The NCCL RAS probe: it ran in both attempts at a 600 s cadence taking 69-83 ms, and the 00:29:43.8Z poll *succeeded during the hang*, so process 0 and NCCL's in-process listener were responsive while the gang was wedged. A rank silently falling off the device-kernel path: `RaggedAllToAllThunk::RunCollective` returns `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")` when `xla_gpu_allow_ragged_all_to_all_nccl_send_recv_fallback` is false, which is the deployed setting, so such a rank fails loudly rather than desynchronising quietly, and no attempt logged an error. Two ragged kernels sharing barrier slots: the hero forces `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, so collectives cannot be co-resident.

**The version skew, which is a real defect on its own.** `tensorflow.bazelrc:192` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim then forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on `ncclTeamLsa(comm).nRanks == comm->nRanks`. That explains structurally why `SupportsGin()` is false — it was never a configuration choice — and why the device kernel only ever runs on the per-rack EP64 clique, so eleven racks are eleven independent barrier domains whose hazard adds with rack count while nothing couples them. It also means the deployed kernel is compiled without 2.30's bounded `sync(..., timeoutCycles)` overload and without its system-scope release fence in `arrive`, which is exactly why the stall cannot report itself.

**Leading remaining hypothesis.** A stray peer store from the copy loop landing inside the devComm resource window and corrupting the barrier state. Every symmetric window, including the one holding the barrier epochs, lives in the same `devr` VA reservation with a common `stride4G`, and the barrier epoch is an absolute per-slot counter that is never reset or exchanged, so any divergence is permanent: a peer that falls behind makes its partner spin on a comparison that wraps to ~2^32, with `abortFlag == nullptr` for user devComms and no timeout. One sub-case has a matching upstream fix we do not carry: NCCL `0d7243b`, "Mitigate loadConst `__ldg` regression", replaces the non-coherent `__ldg` read of `lsaFlatBase`/`stride4G` with a plain dereference, and those window pointers are rewritten at run time by `ncclDevrReplaceSegmentWindowsIfNeeded`.

**Instrumentation now exists, and did not before.** `CUDA_` was missing from the dispatcher's forwarded env prefixes, so the GPU core-dump variables could never reach a training gang; with that fixed the driver creates one dump pipe per rank. A dump must be taken with `CUDA_COREDUMP_GENERATION_FLAGS=skip_abort,skip_global_memory,skip_constbank_memory`: the default writes 62 GB and SIGABRTs the process, which killed all 64 ranks of a smoke gang and lost the dump with the pod, while the flags give 283 MB. Even so it is terminal within about two minutes (measured at 2:36 and 1:55), so it must trigger, read and upload in one round trip and go last. A dump taken mid-kernel names the resident kernel and gives a per-block state table, which matters because the LSA barrier is per-slot indexed by `blockIdx.x` and that table therefore names the diverged slots directly. NCCL RAS `VERBOSE STATUS` can also be triggered by hand during a hang, answering in ~4 ms with the per-collective min/max that showed the AllReduce skew of exactly 3. Do not attach `cuda-gdb` to a live process: an attach to PID 1 returned nothing in 150 s and took the gang down.

**Next.** A wheel built with the device kernels compiled against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7 exists as `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-ca0716a2da95`; it removes the skew, adds bounded LSA barriers that record rank, slot and phase, extends the bounds check to the device path, and promotes the transport line to INFO. It is being validated on one rack. The one structural difference between the hero and the reproduction that survives all of the above is that the hero runs `broadcast_one_to_all` inside `checkpointer.on_step` on every step — a cross-host collective on a `(176, 4)` mesh whose rank groups exist nowhere else in the job — while the reproduction, with `save_checkpoints=False`, never creates a checkpointer at all (`train.py:1031`). A next window should restore that at zero I/O cost with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, and a one-rack `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,REG` A/B on that flag would first confirm the communicator inventory actually differs.

🤖 One actionable gap found while testing a prediction of the barrier-stall hypothesis, worth recording separately because it is cheap to fix and independent of everything else above.

The hypothesis predicts the stuck rack's GPUs were saturated during the hang, spinning inside a resident device kernel, as opposed to idle because the kernel never launched. That is directly checkable from `iris.task`, which carries `accelerator_util_pct` and `accelerator_mem_bytes`. During attempt 0's hang window (00:23:36-00:38:43Z) **both fields are null in all 2,636 samples**.

The query is sound: the same rows reproduce the known CPU signature exactly, with the stuck rack at 4.04 cores against 7.85 on the healthy racks, matching the 4.0-vs-8.0 split reported in this issue. So the nulls are a collection gap rather than a query error.

That gap is expensive out of proportion to its size. GPU utilisation separates "spinning in a resident kernel" from "kernel never launched" on its own, which is the first branch any analysis of this failure has to take, and it needs no core dump, no rebuilt wheel and no reproduction. Enabling accelerator telemetry on the hero gang is the cheapest single change that would improve the next occurrence.

🤖 Follow-up with the experimental record from the overnight session. Four more mechanisms eliminated, three of them by direct experiment rather than inference, and two of them hypotheses raised in this issue's earlier comments. Root cause still not determined; what follows is what a next attempt should not spend time on.

**Residency starvation is refuted.** The concern that the ragged kernel's grid cannot stay fully resident is real in principle — the LSA barrier makes CTA k wait on CTA k of every peer, and a CTA that is never scheduled stalls its peers forever, while the already-resident CTAs spin holding their SMs and never yield, so nothing can free what the missing CTAs need. The pre-patch wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-20260828-c9526e8c0272` is maximally exposed to this: it sizes the grid as `kGridSmMultiplier * core_count` where `kGridSmMultiplier = kRaggedAllToAllDeviceKernelCtasPerSm = 8`, i.e. 1216 CTAs against exactly 1216 CTA slots at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)`. Zero headroom, and its own comment states the requirement. Run at hero shape on one rack it completed **176 steps, roughly 8,400 ragged launches each needing all 1216 CTAs resident simultaneously, with no stall**. Foreign occupancy during the ragged kernel is therefore effectively zero and starvation at the shipped wheel's 8x margin is implausible.

Incidentally, that wheel is about 11% faster: 16.4 s/it and 23.8% MFU against the shipped 18.3 s/it and 21.5%. The grid patch buys a margin this result suggests is not needed, which is worth revisiting on its own merits.

**The autotune-cache race is not this.** The shared node-local `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune` race (#8896) is real and caused a hero retry, but it cannot reach the train step: a 40-step run at a never-compiled shape wrote **zero** autotune results, because this model's heavy GEMMs are Marin's own CUTLASS kernels rather than XLA-autotuned fusions. Autotuning fires only for incidental ops such as the checkpoint slice, so divergent results there cannot change the train step's fusion selection, buffer assignment, arena size or window registration.

**Cross-rack GDR cannot corrupt the barrier.** `devr->lsaFlatBase` is a dedicated `cuMemAddressReserve`; NCCL's network buffers are separate `ncclCudaCalloc` allocations registered through `ncclNetRegMr`. A NIC can only write inside a registered memory region, and a write outside it is rejected by hardware with a completion error rather than landing silently elsewhere.

**Divergent devComm Requirements would be the cleanest mechanism, and both routes to it are closed.** Two ranks requesting different `Requirements` get different devComms, hence different barrier buffers, and since devComm creation is collective each would wait in a barrier the other never joins — silent and permanent, needing no epoch divergence at all. But divergent `lsa_size` takes the `has_remote_peers && !SupportsGin()` branch and fails loudly with `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")`, and no hero rank logged an error; while divergent `core_count` would be a static per-node property, and the failure moved between two node sets the forensics established are disjoint.

**The kernel's copy loops are bounded.** Both the LSA loop and the inner copy terminate on `num_lsa_updates` and `hi` respectively, `hi` is clamped to each update's own extent, and the GIN branch is dead in this build. Combined with the eliminations above, the barrier is the only place this can hang — that part is now established by construction rather than inference.

**Reproduction attempts, all null:** eleven racks at hero shape (235 steps); maximum executable churn with four executables cycling (~300 steps); registration determinism (all 64 ranks byte-identical, 29 registrations, same order and offsets); cold autotune at a novel shape; zero-headroom residency (176 steps); four EP cliques on one rack (189 steps); and a second transfer geometry at `--latent-dim 2048 --capacity-factor 1.37`, which changes stride and alignment in every offset the copy computes (192 steps).

A single rack cannot reach the remaining space, and the reason is structural: symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so extra communicators and expert-domain splitting do not emulate eleven racks. Closing this needs the failure state observed. The capture path is now armed by default on the ragged transport, so the next occurrence should name itself rather than produce fifteen minutes of silence.

🤖 Correction to a recommendation I left in an earlier comment. I suggested a one-rack A/B on `--save-checkpoints` to confirm that the hero's per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` creates a communicator inventory the reproduction lacks. I have now run it, and that test cannot work on one rack. Anyone picking this up should not spend a window on it.

Ran at hero shape with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, which exercises the collective without ever performing the 5.4 TB write, and with the step-sharding fix disabled: 164 steps, 16.9 s/it, no stall.

The reason it is not a real test is in the counter. `Init COMPLETE` appears **64 times, once per rank — a single communicator**. At one rack the `(16, 4)` process mesh *is* the same 64 ranks as the expert-parallel clique, so `broadcast_one_to_all` reuses that communicator and creates no distinct rank group. At eleven racks the mesh is `(176, 4)` and spans all 704 ranks, so its rank groups exist nowhere else in the job. The structural difference I wanted to probe only exists at multi-rack, so a clean single-rack result says nothing about it either way.

That matters beyond this one experiment, because it closes the single-rack search on structural grounds rather than by exhaustion of ideas. Two independent reasons now, both measured:

- Symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so additional communicators and expert-domain splitting add no window pressure and do not emulate eleven racks.
- The last identified per-step difference, the checkpointer's `broadcast_one_to_all`, collapses onto the expert-parallel clique at `(16, 4)`.

Note also that `save_checkpoints=False` means no checkpointer object is constructed at all (`train.py:1031`), so every reproduction attempt in this issue executed that collective exactly zero times. That remains the only per-step structural difference between the configuration that hung twice and the ones that did not — it simply cannot be tested below eleven racks.

Nothing here changes the standing conclusion: the locus is established (the kernel's copy loops are bounded, so the barrier is the only place this can hang) and the unreportability is explained, but the trigger is undetermined and needs the failure state observed. The capture path is armed by default on the ragged transport, so a recurrence should name itself.

🤖 Retitled from "hangs on one rack at d6144 hero scale after a watch step" to drop the watch-step attribution, which the evidence no longer supports.

The original framing was that two executables — a plain train step and a `diagnostic_watch_step` — alias the symmetric-memory arena, and that the hang lands on the first plain step after a watch step. The deployed commit sets `WatchMode.INLINE` (`launch_scaling_ladder.py:216`), so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built: `jit_train_step` computes the watch statistics on every step and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. The hanging step was byte-identical to the step before it.

The timing correlation is also weaker than the title implied. With `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, attempt 1 completed step 54000, a watch-boundary step, and hung on 54001 — immediately after.
