🤖 Result of the 2026-09-04 eleven-rack telemetry window. No hang in 183 job-steps, but the new barrier instrumentation produced the first *measured* asymmetry between racks this issue has had, and it is not hardware.

**What ran.** `mcwitt/8870-repro` @ `0ee0880b77`, which is the hung commit `8e48cdb3ca` plus diagnostics and nothing else (not rebased; the six main-line commits past `8e48cdb3ca` touch no training code). PJRT wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-3091aa7302d8`: device kernels built against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7, both LSA barrier waits bounded at ~45 s with a record naming rank, slot and phase on expiry, and — new for this run — a per-thunk, per-phase high-water mark of the barrier wait, logged at INFO whenever it doubles above 1 ms. Hero-identical otherwise: the #8861 fix switched off so both aliasing windows are present (confirmed two per rank), the checkpointer constructed with a 600-minute interval so its per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` runs, `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NVLS`, core dump armed. Restored `step-54000`, 11 racks / 704 GPUs / batch 11264, system priority. Steps 54000–54183 at 17–19 s/it and 23% MFU, loss 1.2364 at 54000 exactly as in both hero attempts. Zero barrier timeouts, zero bounds violations, zero errors. The JAX compilation cache hit with the new wheel, since the cache key does not include the PJRT build (`cache_key.py` hashes `jaxlib`'s version and `platform_version`, which is the CUDA runtime), so startup was six minutes.

**The measurement.** Post-copy waits never exceed 4.2 ms on any rank. Pre-copy waits on racks 0–7 (tasks 0–127) never exceed 10.5 ms, with per-rack medians of 5.6–9.9 ms. Pre-copy waits on racks 8, 9 and 10 (tasks 128–175) reach **158, 103 and 128 ms**, with per-rack medians of 157, 98 and 124 ms — i.e. essentially every rank on those three racks saw it. Full sweep of all 704 ranks is in `scratch/8870/window/w3-waitmarks.csv`.

**Event structure.** Collapsing the ≥50 ms lines by timestamp gives six events during the run (a seventh at 23:31:46 coincides with the cancel at 23:31:50 and is teardown). Each is a single launch on a single rack in which **63 of the 64 ranks wait the same ~N ms** — so one rank arrived late to the pre-copy barrier and its 63 clique peers waited for it. The rank that did not wait is the straggler, and it is a different rank on a different node every time:

| time (UTC) | rack | waiters | median wait | rank that did not wait | node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 22:36:36 | 9 | 63 | 98 ms | task 145 rank 3 | `s4gwxs64` |
| 22:36:56 | 8 | 63 | 101 ms | task 136 rank 2 | `s8mtxs64` |
| 22:37:29 | 10 | 63 | 81 ms | task 168 rank 2 | `s9jyxs64` |
| 22:38:33 | 8 | 45 | 52 ms | (19 below threshold) | — |
| 22:40:30 | 10 | 63 | 124 ms | task 162 rank 3 | `s2grxs64` |
| 22:45:18 | 8 | 63 | 158 ms | task 134 rank 3 | `s7qvxs64` |

Roughly steps 2, 2, 3, 8, 13 and 28. Six different nodes, six different ranks, three racks, never racks 0–7. A bad GPU or host would recur on itself; this roams. And these are sticky maxima that only log on a doubling, so a repeat at the same magnitude is invisible — the true event count is at least this and probably higher.

**Placement.** The task-to-node map was identical to the hero's own 176-task placement and to last night's second window; the first window differed at rack indices 0 and 1, so the index is "whichever racks are free" and is not a stable identifier. What is stable: rack 8 here is **the same sixteen nodes, 16 of 16, as the slice that stalled in hero attempt 0** (tasks 128–143, `s38vxs64 … shmsxs64`), and racks 9 and 10 were the same physical nodes in every one of these placements too. So this data cannot separate "the last three replica indices" from "these three specific racks". Against the hardware reading: attempt 1's stuck slice (tasks 64–79, rack 4) shows nothing here, 7.6 ms maximum, indistinguishable from the healthy racks.

**Reading it, carefully.** Pre-copy is the rendezvous before any peer store, so a long pre-copy wait means EP-clique peers had not yet *reached* the ragged kernel; the copies themselves are not slow (post-copy is flat). One rank per event arriving 80–160 ms late, recurring, only on replica indices 8–10 of the 11-wide `replica_dcn` axis, points at something rank-order-dependent upstream of the all-to-all: the two `nranks 11` replica-axis communicators that rank 0 reports (ring or tree position of the last three replicas), the data loader's per-replica shard timing, the checkpointer's `(176, 4)` broadcast that was live for the first time in a reproduction, or host-side work that lands on those ranks. None of that is tested. What it is not: a hang — 160 ms is three orders of magnitude short of 45 s, and in 183 steps nothing grew toward one. Whether the hang is the extreme tail of this distribution or a different phenomenon is exactly the open question, but until now there was no distribution to speak of.

**Also recorded from this run.** Communicator inventory on rank 0 with the checkpointer live: `nranks 64`, `704`, and two `nranks 11`. Two arena windows per rank (1408 across 704 ranks), as in the hang. `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG` was dropped after measuring that it alone produced 98.5% of task-log volume (one `IPC reuse buffer` line per collective per peer, 356 MB per task per hour, ~63 GB per window into finelog); without it a task logs ~5 MB. The hero resumed from the forced `step-61806` at 23:35Z and is running.

**Next.** (1) Make recurrence measurable: a per-launch histogram, or reset the marks every N launches, so the event rate and its trend over a longer run are observable rather than inferred from doublings. (2) Separate position from hardware: a placement that lands different physical racks at replica indices 8–10 — the Kueue gate that blocked today's smoke (#8925) makes this awkward but it is the decisive test. (3) Catch the straggler in the act: a host-side timestamp around the ragged thunk on every rank would say what the late rank was doing — the barrier marks say only that it was late. (4) Repeat with the #8861 fix on, to see whether one executable per rank changes the tail.

🤖 The hung run pinned a QuACK version with a concrete matrix-multiplication (GEMM) scheduler defect. This is a new lead; the cause of #8870 remains unproved.

The deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca` [pins QuACK 0.6.1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L96), and the archived attempt-0 task-1 setup log confirms `quack-kernels==0.6.1`. The ragged backend's [activation GEMMs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic_cute.py#L57) use Cluster Launch Control (CLC), which lets resident GPU thread blocks take over work from pending clusters, with variable-length expert groups. The audited package source matches the [0.6.1 release](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/02c7f69881737731173a6a009aeb6f032e449b61/quack/tile_scheduler.py#L504).

That scheduler can observe a failed CLC cancellation, leave its work loop, and then issue more cancellations through its unconditional `cancel_pending_tail` path. NVIDIA's [PTX specification](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#parallel-synchronization-and-communication-instructions-clusterlaunchcontrol-try-cancel) defines further cancellation requests after a GPU thread block observes failure as undefined behavior. The drain also issues asynchronous requests without waiting for their responses before exit.

Upstream [58cb592a1a6e](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6e) replaces this path with a conditional, response-checked drain and a separate response buffer. Its [investigation](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/58cb592a1a6e/AI/clc_spurious_invalid_investigation.md) reports stale GEMM output tiles with a second process sharing the GPU and multiple queued GEMM launches, plus a separate GPU-error hazard from requests still in flight at block exit. Those experiments used B300; they do not establish the behavior of our GB200 run. The specification violation does not prove it caused our silent hang, and the cached GPU binary from the original run has not yet been checked against that source.

If this defect prevents a rank's GEMM from completing, the other ranks in its expert-parallel group could wait indefinitely at the next ragged barrier. The [earlier bounded-copy-loop argument](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5537281960) does not exclude a preceding kernel that never completes. Next is a comparison of the original scheduler and a narrow drain fix under finite competing GPU work, checking for incorrect outputs, timeouts and GPU errors at the production matrix dimensions. Each version will use a separate compilation cache so the treatment executes newly compiled code.

🤖 The production hero — on the **pooled-wave** transport, not ragged — stalled silently for fifteen minutes today and then died of an NVLink fault, and it originated on one of the three racks the telemetry window flagged. This is the strongest evidence so far that #8870's root cause is a fabric fault on specific NVL72 domains rather than anything in the ragged kernel, which merely fails silently where NCCL's host path eventually fails loudly.

**Timeline (2026-09-05, UTC), `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` on the same 176 nodes and the same rack map as both 09-02 hang attempts and the 09-04 window.** Last step 65069 completed at 17:19:31. Nothing was logged by any rank for the next fifteen minutes; Iris's py-spy dumps at 17:21 and 17:31 show every sampled rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), i.e. blocked on the device — the #8870 shape exactly. At **17:34:36.549 task 162 rank 1 on `s2grxs64` (rack 10, NVLink domain `dh1-r137`)** logged the first `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (from `cudaFreeAsync`, `gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the other rack-10 nodes followed within 0.5 s, racks 2 and 6 by 17:34:37.8, and every rack by 17:34:43 — 88 of 176 tasks logged the fault, the rest were taken down by fate sharing. Iris restarted the gang; it resumed from the hourly temp `step-64944` at 17:38, so the event cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. It is healthy again (step 65623 at 20 s/step).

**Why this bears on the ragged hangs.** The pooled-wave transport moves data through NCCL's host-driven path, where a fabric fault eventually surfaces as a contained CUDA error and the driver tears the context down. The ragged device kernel spins in an LSA barrier with `abortFlag == nullptr` and, on the wheel that hung, no bounded wait, so the same fault produces fifteen minutes of silence followed by the 900 s progress watchdog — which is what both 09-02 attempts looked like. The fifteen-minute latency before the contained error is itself notable: the fault was in progress, invisible, for as long as the ragged hangs lasted before the watchdog fired.

**The three racks now line up with three independent fabric observations.** Rack 10 (`dh1-r137`): today's fault origin; and `s2grxs64` is the node that supplied the 22:40:30 straggler in the window (task 162, 124 ms). Rack 8 (`dh1-r129`): the 09-02 attempt-0 stall node set; a 5.009 s NVLS multicast bind at window startup (9-12× every other rack); the only repeat straggler node; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 is a flapping NVLink — 505 recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample last night and +1 more since, read-only from the running hero, the only counter that moved anywhere in a five-rack sweep. Rack 9 (`dh1-r136`): stragglers in the window, no counter evidence yet. Racks 0-7 show none of this. Rack 10's own GPU-side link counters did not move across today's fault, so the error is on the switch side or a non-link hardware error; node `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from inside the containers.

**What this changes.** The 09-04 deep-dive (`scratch/8870/window/deepdive/`, eleven streams) had already falsified the cross-rack collective-stall mechanism and left "a per-GPU transient of 25-160 ms, ≥11× more frequent on racks 8-10, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame." A fabric fault that stalls whatever is crossing a link, escalating occasionally to a contained error or a permanent stall, fits every measurement in this issue, including why attempt 0 hung on rack 8 and why one-rack reproductions on healthy racks never reproduced anything. It does not explain attempt 1 (rack 4, `dh1-r124`), which shows nothing in any sweep; that may be a fourth domain or a different event.

**Untested but now less likely as the cause:** the NCCL 2.29.7/2.30.7 compile skew (the ragged wheel that hung compiled its kernels against 2.29.7; every diagnostic wheel since used 2.30.7). It remains the one code difference between the hung configuration and every clean run, and an A/B wheel exists (`marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-355d8f15cc25`), but today's fault happened with no ragged kernel in the picture at all.

🤖 Offline decode of the [September 15 missing-peer dump](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/441) narrows the stall to a self-deadlocked CTA inside QuACK 0.6.4's SM100 grouped GEMM, and identifies the one code path that separates the warps that retired from the warps that did not. QuACK is not exonerated: the rank stops inside this kernel with no external dependency left, and the deadlock is structural to its CLC scheduler. The initiating condition is still unproved, and two reproduction attempts at production shape did not trigger it.

The stuck kernel is the `dh` backward GEMM (`quack_grouped_gemm(dy, w2, cu, b_major="k")`, tile 256x256, cluster 2x2x1, CLC on). Both resident clusters show the same state in every CTA: the MMA warp and all four epilogue warps have exited, the TMA load warp waits on an A/B empty barrier that the exited MMA warp will never release, and the scheduler warp is still inside its CLC loop. The scheduler ring holds three valid grants (work indices 3996/4032/4068 in one cluster, 4011/4047/4083 in the other), and the ring's barrier words show every warp released grants 1-4 while only the four scheduler warps released grant 5. So the MMA and epilogue warps decoded grant 4 as "no more work" and retired, while the load and scheduler warps decoded the same grant as a valid batch-1 tile and kept going. The load warp's registers hold the batch-1 window `[2214, 4182)` (369 and 328 M-clusters for the first two groups), inside which index 4032 is valid; the retired warps must have used a window ending in `(4011, 4032]`. No invalid CLC response was ever in the ring, so this is not the spurious-cancel failure fixed in 0.6.4.

Every warp role decodes its own tile from `cu_seqlens` in global memory (`VarlenMTileScheduler._delinearize_work_idx`, with a per-warp cached batch window). Only the load and scheduler warps execute `griddepcontrol.wait` first (SASS `ACQBULK` at kernel offsets +2272 and +10528); the MMA and epilogue warps' `cu_seqlens` loads (+15408, +21696) come before any wait, and upstream main still has the same placement (`336a5ca` "Enable PDL"). The kernel is launched with PDL (`use_pdl=True` default) and the XLA fusion after it was already resident at its `ACQBULK`, so the sequence is PDL-chained. Under the hero's `save_moe` remat, `cu` is recomputed in the backward by a small fusion, so a predecessor that writes `cu` is plausible. That is the only per-role difference in the decode path and the natural explanation for a role-consistent split, but a one-time stale read at kernel start does not by itself produce the observed state: the retired warps rescan the window at later grants, and a fresh rescan resynchronizes them. The observed state requires those warps to keep seeing stale group boundaries for the whole kernel, which I could not reproduce.

Two probes on `cw-us-east-08a` (2 nodes, production priority, both clean, `/mwittmann/8870-quack-pdl-repro-2` and `/mwittmann/8870-quack-moe-bwd-probe-1`): (1) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_pdl_repro.py`, the production `dh` GEMM at 601,088 rows with the routing alternating every launch so a stale decode is visibly wrong, six arms (production config, PDL off, CLC off, QuACK patched to wait in the MMA/epilogue warps, constant routing, and the `cu` writer as the immediate predecessor), 600 launches per GPU per arm on 8 GPUs, 28,800 launches, zero hangs and zero output mismatches; (2) `experiments/grug/recovery/quack_moe_bwd_probe.py`, the full `_expert_mlp_quack_wgrad` forward plus backward with a fresh random routing every iteration, 1,500 iterations per GPU on 8 GPUs, 72,000 GEMM launches, zero hangs, zero non-finite values. The hero rate is roughly one hang per 1e6 GPU-steps, about 3e-9 per GEMM launch, so a clean 1e5 launches neither confirms nor excludes the PDL path. In probe (1) the PDL-off arm ran at the same speed as production (27 ms versus 27 ms per launch), so disabling PDL on these launchers costs nothing measurable at this shape.

What this changes: the pooled-wave backend runs dense einsums and never touches this kernel, which matches its clean record. CLC off alone removes the per-grant decode (the scheduler warp decodes once and broadcasts) but leaves the initial-tile decode per warp, so it converts most of this failure into wrong or missing tiles rather than a hang, at the 5-12% GEMM cost recorded in `sonic_cute.py`. The cheap, targeted mitigation for the next hero restart is `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers (or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, arm `patched`, to propose upstream); its efficacy can only be judged by the hang recurrence interval, currently one to two thousand steps.
🤖 The latest capture and repeat-snapshot findings are recorded in [the September 15 incident report](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/444).

🤖 Decoding the step-108711 dump (`/tmp/8870-watch-108711/`, task 90) the same way as the step-107501 one adds two facts that the earlier dump could not give, because this one has seven stuck clusters instead of two.

Six of the seven clusters split at a shared threshold. Their scheduler rings hold grants 4305-4404, the load and scheduler warps hold the fresh windows (group 1 is work indices `[2220, 4398)`, group 2 is `[4398, 6558)`; both are in the load warps' `R7/R8/R9` and the scheduler warps' `R8/R9`), and the ring barrier counts show which grant the MMA and epilogue warps retired on: 4358, 4363, 4365, 4340, 4362, 4367 after accepting 4324, 4328, 4332, 4305, 4327, 4333. The retired warps' end of work therefore sits in `(4333, 4340]` in all six clusters, one value, 58-64 indices short of the real end of group 1. That is one stale set of group boundaries shared by 24 CTAs on 24 SMs, not per-CTA noise.

The seventh cluster (blocks 12-13, initial work index 6) is stuck on its very first tile. Its load warp holds the fresh group-0 window `[0, 2220)` and has filled six A/B stages of tile 6 that were never consumed (A/B full parity 1, empty parity 0 in every stage), its scheduler ring holds one grant (index 13, released by the four scheduler warps only), and its MMA and epilogue warps are gone. The MMA warp exited before issuing a single MMA, so it decoded the initial tile, `idx 6 < 2220`, as no work. That is a decode from `cu_seqlens` that says the kernel has fewer than seven clusters of work, taken in the first microseconds of the kernel, by exactly the warps that do not execute `griddepcontrol.wait`. This case needs no persistence argument at all, which was the gap in the previous comment: a stale read at kernel start deadlocks the CTA on its first tile directly. The six other clusters show the same read at a slightly later moment, with `cu_seqlens[1]` already current and the later boundaries not, which fits a buffer being written while the non-waiting warps read it.

One correction to the earlier reading of the scheduler warps: they are parked at the CLC throttle `bar.sync` (kernel offset +11968) waiting for a load-warp credit that never comes, and the reported PC is the following `TRYWAIT`. With that, every barrier count in both dumps reconciles (loads on the tile the MMA warp abandoned, scheduler one credit ahead).

Taken together with the SASS (only the load and scheduler warps wait before their first `cu_seqlens` load), I now put the PDL-stale-input mechanism well above the alternatives. The `cu_seqlens` read the monitoring agent added to the capture is the confirming measurement: on the next hang, the buffer should hold the boundaries the load warp used (`[0, 2220)` and `[2220, 4398)` in work-index units are 370 and 363 M-clusters of 256 rows) while the retired warps evidently used a set that ended around 723 clusters in total. Independently of that read, `use_pdl=False` on the three `quack_moe_cute` launchers, or the two-line wait in the MMA and epilogue warps, is the change to trial at the next relaunch.

🤖 The hero now runs as `hero-nopdl-step108k` (coordinator `/marin/hero-nopdl-step108k-coord-d446fca8`, trainer `/marin/hero-nopdl-step108k-coord-d446fca8/grug-train-hero-nopdl-step108k`, main `8f6f33bebe`), continuing `hero-mix-996f4891-step108k` from its checkpoint `step-108778` with the QuACK grouped GEMMs launched without PDL (#9183) and the PJRT `708c3a4` wheel (#9179). Capture tooling keyed to the previous trainer path needs re-pointing; a hang on this run tests the PDL mechanism directly, since the MMA and epilogue warps can no longer read `cu_seqlens` ahead of the preceding kernel. Trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/hero-nopdl-step108k:-PDL-off-QuACK-launchers-+-PJRT-708c3a4-wheel,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzk0MTE3NQ==

🤖 The latest no-progress alert was traced to a checkpoint error followed by shutdown; it does not establish another GPU-hang recurrence. Details and evidence are in [the incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/459).

🤖 The September 18 UTC stall at step 118837 followed an InfiniBand port failure. Its RAS signature differs from the earlier GPU hangs; no CUDA debugger was attached. The automatic retry restored checkpoint 118722 and resumed training. [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/470). Monitoring continues with the two-minute threshold and the updated capture ready.

🤖 The September 18 stall after step 120206 was another permanent-checkpoint metadata deletion failure. Checkpoint 120000’s pending `DeleteObjects: AccessDenied` surfaced at the next checkpoint synchronization. The automatic retry restored 120000 and resumed training, rolling back 206 steps. [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/473). The metadata commit incompatibility remains; this event provides no GPU-state evidence of an 8870 recurrence. Monitoring continues on attempt 3.

🤖 The September 19 interruption after step 124715 began with `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED` on task 14, local GPU 3, followed by GPU-reset-required and NVLink-mask node conditions. The error leaves invalid peer-memory access versus hardware/driver fault unresolved. No RAS or debugger capture is available, so this does not confirm another silent #8870 hang. Iris automatically retried from checkpoint 124642; attempt 1 resumed and later passed 127172. Evidence and recovery: [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/488).

Permanent checkpoint 126000 subsequently logged successful completion with the deployed metadata fix, and later temporary checkpoints also completed. This verifies permanent publication; restoring 126000 has not been tested. [Checkpoint incident update](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/473). The 120-second no-progress monitor is rearmed on attempt 1 with the updated capture ready.

🤖 The September 23 stall on `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` was traced to rank 0 waiting in an S3 `put_object` for checkpoint 146585’s `manifest.json`. Two host-thread captures showed the same stack. NCCL reported only rank 0 behind, unlike the previously captured rack-wide GPU hangs; no CUDA debugger was attached. Why the S3 call remained blocked is unresolved.

The existing watchdog terminated the stalled attempt, and Iris automatically started attempt 1. All 176 tasks were running by 00:00:27 UTC September 24. The retry restored temporary checkpoint 146355 at 00:01:55, rolling back 228 steps from the last observed metric, then resumed training through step 146366. The two-minute monitor is rearmed. [Incident and evidence](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/518).

topics.title: [iris/grug] Save completed steps on preemption
topics.head: a86084d136d466b68da0613c21eeef2d8e615c44
topics.body:
Grug training ranks now agree on the completed step after SIGTERM and commit that step's model, optimizer, and data-position checkpoint before exiting. A pending asynchronous save completes first; background pruning does not delay shutdown. The `moe_pipeline` and `moe_hero_pipeline` entry points use the same stop decision, while `recovery` writes its final local snapshot. A preempted trainer exits with SIGTERM status after the save so Iris can retry instead of recording partial training as complete.

The shutdown budget is a typed `termination_grace` duration on `IrisClient.submit` and Fray's `JobRequest`, with `--termination-grace` on `iris job run`. The controller resolves a 10-second default, validates the 1-110-second range, and persists the duration through retries and federation. Grug explicitly requests 60 seconds. The supervisor receives that budget; workers and Pods permit five additional seconds for teardown. Container discovery preserves the budget when a worker adopts a running task. Iris generates the supervisor's internal metadata; application environment variables cannot set the infrastructure budget.

At `6279f37`, a [two-H100 Grug base probe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774#issuecomment-6501275454) ran separate preemption trials during a step and during a pending async save. Both committed step 3, restored the model, optimizer, and example position, and matched uninterrupted step-6 state and batch hashes under deterministic GPU settings. Supervisor exit took 8.75 seconds during a step and 10.22 seconds during the async save; a stalled commit was force-killed after 61.12 seconds. The probe used about 0.94 MiB of checkpoint state. Production-size timing, automatic Iris retry, and live worker/Pod shutdown remain unvalidated; workers/controllers were not redeployed.

Part of #10761

comments.body: Working on this in loom: https://loom.oa.dev/s/dm0r86hv

🤖 Holistic review of d63c66ccf2898d7b95635af08ee0ea5a4a391e8d.

This change makes Grug trainers stop at an agreed completed step on SIGTERM and commit a permanent checkpoint before exiting. It also lets Iris give such tasks a longer shutdown budget. The checkpoint path is sound. However, a preempted single-process run now exits 0, and Iris can record that as success. I recommend fixing that before merge.

**Before.** SIGTERM killed the trainer immediately. The task exited with 143 (or the multi-GPU supervisor returned 128+SIGTERM). Iris marked the attempt failed or preempted and retried from the last periodic checkpoint. The supervisor's grace was a hard-coded 10 s, and the worker's kill wait was 5 s.

**Design.** `experiments/grug/preemption.py` records SIGTERM, then allgathers `(completed_step, requested)` after each step so every rank breaks at the same step. The Levanter-backed variants call the new `Checkpointer.save_final_checkpoint`. It waits for any pending async save and forces a permanent save unless that step already has one. Background pruning is not awaited. The pipeline variants and the recovery diagnostic save directly. On the Iris side, `IRIS_PREEMPTION_GRACE_SECONDS` drives three settings: the `multigpu_main` SIGKILL deadline, the worker's `TaskAttempt.kill` wait (grace + 5 s), and the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (grace + 5 s). During a graceful kill, the worker monitor no longer force-kills. A container that exits with 0, 143, or 137 after a stop request is reported as KILLED. Grug dispatch defaults the grace to 60 s.

**Evidence and limits.** I ran the changed tests locally and they pass: the worker graceful-kill and reconcile tests, the pod-manifest test, `test_multigpu`, the Levanter final-checkpoint test, and the Grug SIGTERM-recording test. As the body says, no controlled preemption ran, so the 60 s budget and the remote-storage commit time are unmeasured.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `experiments/grug/base/train.py:648` (and the same `else:` branch in `moe`, `moe_hero_ep`, `moe_hero_fsdp`, `fast_track`, plus `moe_pipeline/train.py:388` and `moe_hero_pipeline/pipeline_smoke.py:568`). After a preemption break the trainer saves and then returns normally, so the process exits 0. Only the multi-GPU supervisor (`processes_per_task > 1`) turns an external signal into `128 + signum`. Every other Grug task, including all TPU runs and single-process GPU runs, reports a clean exit. On Kubernetes, a Kueue-preempted pod whose container exits 0 reaches phase `Succeeded`. `_task_update_from_pod` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py:1385`) maps that phase to `TASK_STATE_SUCCEEDED` without checking `_disruption_condition`. On the worker backend, a SIGTERM the worker did not send (VM shutdown or `docker stop`) leaves `should_stop` false, so `_monitor_loop` returns SUCCEEDED. In both cases `dispatch_grug_training_run`'s `job.wait()` succeeds, nothing retries, and the executor records a partially trained step as complete. The README promise that "retries … restore the saved step" then never applies. Fix: after the final save on the preempted path, exit with the supervisor's convention (`raise SystemExit(128 + signal.SIGTERM)`, or have `GracefulPreemption` expose the received signum). Add a test that a preempted loop exits non-zero.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/iris/src/iris/preemption.py:13`. A user-set task environment variable now controls infrastructure deadlines in the worker and the pod spec. It is validated only in Grug dispatch and has no upper bound. If a job submitted with `iris job run -e IRIS_PREEMPTION_GRACE_SECONDS abc` is later killed, `TaskAttempt.kill` raises `ValueError` before it signals the container. `_kill_async` swallows that in its thread, so the attempt keeps running as a zombie. A job can also set `86400` and get a one-day `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, which stalls Kueue preemption of its node for that long. Fix: carry the grace as a typed `iris.time.Duration` field on the job and `RunTaskRequest`, next to the existing `timeout = 7`, and on Fray's `JobRequest` next to `timeout`. Have the controller validate and cap it at submission. Then the worker and k8s backend read the field, and Iris injects the env var only for the in-container `multigpu_main` supervisor.
- **3. Should fix:** `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py:765`. `submit_task`'s supersede path calls `current.kill()` synchronously inside the Reconcile handler. It now inherits the grace + 5 s default, which is 65 s for Grug tasks; before, the wait was 5 s and a SIGTERM usually ended the process at once. The controller's `RECONCILE_RPC_TIMEOUT` is 3 s and `worker_unreachable_grace` is 50 s. While this kill waits, each later reconcile re-enters `submit_task`, because the new UID is still unknown, and blocks again. Within one graceful save the worker can be reaped as unreachable. The controller has already abandoned the superseded attempt, so a graceful save adds nothing there. Pass the old explicit bound (`current.kill(term_timeout_ms=5000)`) on this path, or kill it via `_kill_async`.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:d63c66ccf2898d7b95635af08ee0ea5a4a391e8d -->

🤖 Removed five stale callback comments and a redundant test helper docstring. The README now states that the 60-second grace has not been validated. Lint review passed; 19 reconcile tests passed.

<!-- marin-deslop:d63c66ccf2898d7b95635af08ee0ea5a4a391e8d -->

🤖 Addressed the holistic review's retry blocker in 6279f37cd3. After the final checkpoint commits, every Grug training entry point exits with SIGTERM status; an integrated one-step base test checks the nonzero exit and completed checkpoint. The worker now validates the grace value before starting a task, and the shared parser caps it at 110 seconds. The setting remains a launch-time environment override because Iris passes it to the rank supervisor at the task boundary. Superseding an old attempt uses the previous five-second bound so reconciliation does not inherit the longer checkpoint window.

🤖 Controlled GPU checkpoint/restart validation passed for 6279f37cd38a7281c85afe27137eac7216f23f2a in [this Iris job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fgrug-preemption-10761-20261029-v4).

The probe ran the actual Grug base loop with two H100s, one JAX process per GPU, and remote CoreWeave checkpoints. It used an 82,240-parameter synthetic model (about 0.94 MiB of checkpoint state), batch size 4, sequence length 64, and six training steps.

- SIGTERM to the multi-GPU supervisor during a training step and during a pending async save made both ranks stop at completed step 3, commit a permanent checkpoint, and exit with status 143. The async case held the commit callback for five seconds.
- Restarting with the same run ID and checkpoint root restored model and optimizer hashes identical to the saved step-3 state and resumed at example 12. Batch-token hashes matched uninterrupted training, and both restarted runs reached step 6 with bitwise-identical model and optimizer state to the uninterrupted baseline. A newer incomplete `step-999` directory was ignored.
- Time from the SIGTERM request to supervisor exit was 8.75 seconds during a step and 10.22 seconds during the async save. With a deliberately stalled commit callback, the supervisor force-killed both ranks at its configured 60-second deadline and exited after 61.12 seconds. An injected rank failure terminated the group with a nonzero status within 0.86 seconds.

Exact GPU comparisons used `XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` and `JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`. Without that control, independent runs already differed numerically before SIGTERM. The job's uploaded output archive contains `result.json` and rank event records; the permanent remote checkpoint completion markers were also verified.

This validates the small Grug base/supervisor path. Production-size checkpoint timing, automatic Iris task retry, other variants on GPU, and the proposed worker/Pod grace settings remain untested on live infrastructure. Workers/controllers were not redeployed. The proposed 60-second production grace still needs a representative-size measurement.

issue.title: [hero] Record adjusted averaging and compact chat SFT
issue.body:
## TL;DR

Adjusted warmup-stable-merge-inspired checkpoint averaging followed by donor initialization of five chat-token output columns and 64 updates of compact LoRA plus vocabulary SFT produced a provisional Hero checkpoint for short RL capacity-planning trials. On 100 reviewed responses, all stopped at end-of-turn within the 2,048-token cap. Reasoning and code errors remain; this establishes a usable experiment proxy, not heldout quality or serving throughput.

## Description

The goal was to obtain basic thinking and turn-taking without paying for a full-model cooldown. The sequence was latest checkpoint A → LR-adjusted average B → chat-token donor initialization C → compact SFT and merged native export D. The prior investigation is recorded in [Marin #10428](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10428), including checkpoint paths and the [reviewed response gist](https://gist.github.com/dlwh/408759a8eb09796d253b8b53a43769d4).

## Hypothesis or Goal

Test whether weight averaging and a small trainable adapter/vocabulary surface provide a sufficient provisional checkpoint for capacity planning. Compare A/B on identical C4 tokens, measure training-source end-of-turn acquisition, and review 100 fresh math, Python and fixed-history responses. Full heldout quality, merge/serving parity and RL throughput remain separate questions.

## Status

The experiment and response review are complete. The runnable research archive is published at `d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9`, following the research-engineering workflow in Marin #9467. Its full source/history, notebook, original commands, rejected paths and tests remain together on a Marin-derived branch. Two fresh reviewers selected only existing short-convolution gradient, router-bias export and GB200 device-type fixes for continued maintenance in [Marin #10556](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10556). The broad reproduction PR #10539 is superseded.

## Links

- Related investigation: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10428
- Notebook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/notebook.md
- Selection review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/selection.md
- Research source: https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/tree/codex/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft
- Marin contribution (open): https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10556
- WSM reference: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17634
- LoRA reference: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685
- Reviewed responses: https://gist.github.com/dlwh/408759a8eb09796d253b8b53a43769d4

## Decision Log

- Preserve the complete reviewed experimental implementation and meaningful failures in a runnable archive. Historical replay alone does not make the entire campaign harness a maintained Marin API.
- Keep checkpoint paths and original results accessible from the related Marin issue. Use this issue and the commit-pinned notebook as the canonical research narrative.

- Concrete resource collection annotations were excluded from Marin after the caller audit found that their JSON decoder belongs only to the archived campaign. GB200 is retained for the existing native sampler.

## Conclusion

Use the merged step-64 checkpoint provisionally for short RL capacity-planning work. Basic turn-taking was observed in this sample. Correctness errors, two special-token anomalies, training-data reuse and unmeasured serving behavior limit the conclusion. No additional training or inference runs are part of this archival change.

issue.title: [hero] Audit and mitigate attention softmax gradient error
issue.body:
## Completed frozen checkpoint comparison

Genuine FP32 saved attention output reduces measured fused Q/K gradient error on all three Hero checkpoints. At 330k, pooled relative L2 error decreases from 0.9323%/0.8173% to 0.2767%/0.2487%. Upcasting already rounded BF16 O retains baseline error. The fixed-forward shadow gives nearly identical gradient accuracy, with higher measured attention cost. Training-quality impact remains unmeasured; live Hero is unchanged.

| Method: Q / K relative L2 error | 270k | 300k | 330k |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Production baseline | 0.5670% / 0.4006% | 0.6012% / 0.4299% | 0.9323% / 0.8173% |
| Genuine FP32 saved O | 0.2836% / 0.2516% | 0.3303% / 0.2788% | 0.2767% / 0.2487% |
| Fixed-forward shadow | 0.2836% / 0.2516% | 0.3303% / 0.2788% | 0.2767% / 0.2487% |
| Sampled projection prototype | 0.1918% / 0.2135% | 0.1976% / 0.2228% | 0.1841% / 0.2158% |

The [full report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e/logbooks/12-hero-attention-softmax/mitigation-comparison-report.md) contains all six variants, absolute errors, local/global and per-layer results, finite/count checks, distributions, forward differences, dense timings and remaining limits. The [notebook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e/logbooks/12-hero-attention-softmax/notebook.md) preserves the original diagnostic, failed attempts and recovery decisions. [Sanitized numerical summary](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e/logbooks/12-hero-attention-softmax/mitigation-comparison-summary.json.gz), [gradient CSV](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e/logbooks/12-hero-attention-softmax/mitigation-gradient-errors.csv), [timing CSV](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e/logbooks/12-hero-attention-softmax/mitigation-dense-timings.csv), and [runnable research source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/tree/639890bd78bf2455624bc5ad3f105f0f1d8d2a9e).

## Concentrated error and mitigation

At 330k, global layer 15 accounts for 64.59% of baseline Q squared error and 76.07% of K squared error. Layer Q/K relative error decreases from 4.4781%/4.5292% to 0.3465%/0.3233% with FP32 saved O. A matched query-head observation has 45.8507% baseline Q error and accounts for 63.651% of checkpoint Q squared error. Its maximum probability is 0.969517 and margin 3.45964, far below the approximately 16.64 FP32 margin threshold. Audited top-eight absolute-error events bound its repaired Q relative error above by 0.366867% for FP32 O/shadow and 0.246586% for projection; exact repaired row errors were not retained. The bounds use the same-run reference norm.

The candidate retains genuine pre-BF16 O and computes the backward normalization `D = sum(O_fp32 * dO_fp32)`. This is not an upcast of rounded O or a dO-storage change. Its accepted single-query-stage pipeline leaves the production baseline unchanged. The optimized forward changes about 0.062–0.066% of public BF16 output components. The shadow returns baseline public O/LSE and uses a second forward for FP32 auxiliary state. At length 16384, paired attention forward/backward timings cost about 8% more for FP32 O and 34–38% more for the shadow. These are attention-case timings, not full-step throughput. Native-plus-XLA sampled projection has no efficient dense implementation or measured dense cost.

## Method, validation and limits

The frozen comparison uses checkpoints 270000/300000/330000, ten selected local/global layers, 64 rank panels/layer, 48 query heads and four selected queries with full keys. Actual fused GPU Q/K is compared against stable CPU FP64 from identical quantized Q/K/V and real downstream dO from CE plus final-logit z-loss 1e-4. Both gradients derive from the same sparse selected-query objective; dK is not a full-step parameter gradient. Relative error pools squared norms across panels.

Coordinator and worker both succeeded. All 1920 panels, six variants, 368640 multi-key query/head observations and 1152 timing records passed validation. All eleven required captured-tail/baseline/decoder parity and native operand finite/mask/contraction gates are zero. No nonzero-reference whole Q/K vector vanished in any variant. There is only one sampled row above margin 24 ln(2), or 0.0002713%; this is below 0.1% on this attention-margin metric, not a production-token collapse estimate. Samples are correlated. Stored-output controls support attribution without directly observing native internal score gradients or proving training harm.

Earlier independent compilation produced differing native GPU instructions. The compiler root cause remains unresolved. The completed comparison agrees on each compilation request's source/dependencies, order, launcher and runtime/device identity, then distributes and verifies one genuine executable. The ordinary compile guard remained enabled and passed. Validation checked 34 phase provenances, 12480 request proofs and 153 producer object files. Cached scopes can legitimately have no new native calls. This does not prove equivalence of the earlier binaries. Compiler artifacts, full requests, original results and operational metadata remain private; no operand/token arrays are public.

The original narrow-head diagnostic reported 0.5483%/0.3965%, 0.4775%/0.3586%, and 3.1118%/2.4963% Q/K error. Its head coverage and the matched row's reference norm differ from the new all-head comparison. The changed baseline percentage is not mitigation evidence. Constructed two-key cancellation acceptance is also separate from checkpoint prevalence.

## Decision and next ownership

The original diagnostic and frozen mitigation comparison are complete. Genuine FP32 auxiliary O is the leading numerical mitigation; upcasting rounded O was rejected by its unchanged error. The forward-preserving shadow is an accuracy control with measured extra cost. Projection remains an accuracy prototype. This closes the research scope with validated evidence, not a training-quality claim.

Production maintainers should scope an efficient FP32 auxiliary-output implementation, explicitly choose its public-forward parity requirement, and decide whether to authorize a separately bounded paired training continuation with full-step memory, throughput, loss, stability and quality measurements. No additional training or production change is launched here. The completed [output-CE investigation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/10) remains closed. The research branch is preserved; its index-only [PR #14](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/pull/14) must not merge the research source tree into main.
